lead: Emotion is carried less by the words and more by how they are said: pitch rises in anger and happiness, energy drops in sadness, pauses lengthen in fear. So we describe each utterance by summary statistics of pitch, energy and spectral features over its frames, and classify that vector into a label. The labels are usually anger, happiness, sadness, fear, disgust, surprise and neutral. The idea is used to spot upset customers in a call-centre queue. Only a few universities teach this topic.
prereq: You need: 7.5 for MFCC and delta features, 7.3 for spectrograms, and Unit 5 for SVM and classification metrics.

blocks.text: Emotion labels are the six basics — anger, happiness, sadness, fear, disgust, surprise — plus neutral. Words matter little; prosody and voice quality carry most of the signal.

items: F0 (fundamental frequency, the vocal-fold vibration rate in Hz): mean and range rise in anger and happiness, fall in sadness.
Energy (frame loudness): high in anger and happiness, low in sadness.
Speaking rate in syllables per second: faster in anger and happiness, slower in sadness.
Pause length: longer in sadness and fear.

blocks.text: Voice quality adds jitter (cycle-to-cycle variation of the F0 period) and shimmer (cycle-to-cycle variation of amplitude); both rise in tense voices. Spectral shape comes from MFCCs and their deltas (see 7.5).

eGeMAPS is a standard fixed bundle of such low-level descriptors. Corpora are acted (actors perform the emotion) or natural (real recordings). Acted speech is easier; scores drop on natural speech. Always state whether testing is speaker-dependent or speaker-independent.

sections.h3: From frames to an utterance vector

items: Frame the signal: 25 ms frames with a 10 ms hop.
Compute frame features: F<sub>0</sub>, energy, 13 MFCCs and their deltas.
Summarise each feature over the utterance's voiced frames by mean, standard deviation, minimum and maximum.
Classify the summarised vector: an SVM with an RBF kernel is the baseline; a CNN on the spectrogram (see 7.3) or an LSTM on the frame sequence is the neural alternative.

blocks.text: Evaluation uses a confusion matrix C, where C[i][j] counts utterances of true class i predicted as class j.
accuracy = (1/N) Σ C[i][i]     recall(i) = C[i][i] / Σ C[i][j]     UAR = (1/K) Σ recall(i)
blocks.where: N is the number of test utterances, K the number of emotion classes, C the confusion matrix with C[i][j] = utterances of true class i predicted as class j; sums run over i or j as shown. UAR (unweighted average recall) gives every class equal weight, whatever its size.

figure.caption: Rows are the true emotions, columns the predictions. The diagonal holds 32, 28 and 20, so each class has recall 0.80, and accuracy and unweighted average recall are both 0.80.

examples.question: A test set has 100 utterances: 40 angry, 35 happy, 25 neutral. The classifier gets angry 32 right (5 as happy, 3 as neutral), happy 28 right (4 as angry, 3 as neutral) and neutral 20 right (2 as angry, 3 as happy). Find accuracy, per-class recall and unweighted average recall.
steps: Row sums check: 32+5+3 = 40 angry; 4+28+3 = 35 happy; 2+3+20 = 25 neutral; total = 100.
examples.check:
correct = {'angry': 32, 'happy': 28, 'neutral': 20}
total = {'angry': 40, 'happy': 35, 'neutral': 25}
acc = sum(correct.values()) / sum(total.values())
print(f"{acc:.2f}")
recalls = []
for k in ['angry', 'happy', 'neutral']:
    r = correct[k] / total[k]
    recalls.append(r)
    print(f"{r:.2f}")
uar = sum(recalls) / len(recalls)
print(f"{uar:.2f}")

traps: Reporting accuracy with imbalanced classes: always answering 'angry' scores 0.40 here with no skill. Report UAR.
Splitting by utterance instead of by speaker leaks the speaker's voice into test data and inflates the score.
Acted-corpus scores do not transfer to natural calls; state the corpus and the split.
F0 in Hz depends on speaker sex and age, so absolute values are not comparable across speakers.
High energy alone does not mean anger — happiness raises it too. Arousal is easier than valence.

quiz.q: Name the seven emotion labels used here.
quiz.a: Anger, happiness, sadness, fear, disgust, surprise, neutral.
Jitter is cycle-to-cycle variation of the F0 period; shimmer is cycle-to-cycle variation of amplitude.

quiz.q: Why summarise frames into utterance statistics?
quiz.a: Emotion lasts over the utterance and classifiers need a fixed-length vector; mean, standard deviation, minimum and maximum do this.

quiz.q: A test set has 20 sad and 60 neutral utterances. A model gets 10 sad and 55 neutral right. Find accuracy and UAR.
Why can an always-'angry' classifier score 40 % accuracy but low UAR?
quiz.a: Accuracy is dominated by the largest class. UAR averages recall over classes, and the classes never predicted get recall 0.

quiz.q: Give two reasons speaker-independent scores are lower than speaker-dependent ones.
quiz.a: F0 range and voice quality differ across speakers, and a model can memorise speaker identity, which fails on new speakers.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry uses emotion recognition in call-centre triage, driver monitoring and mental-health screening. Research has moved to self-supervised speech models fine-tuned for emotion, and to dimensional labels (arousal and valence) instead of discrete classes. Search 'eGeMAPS' and 'unweighted average recall'.
